items.stem: What is the aim of supply-side policies?
options: To increase the productive capacity of the economy
To increase AD in the short run
items.answer: To increase the productive capacity of the economy
items.markingKey: Shift LRAS right.

items.stem: Explain how privatisation might increase the efficiency of an industry.
items.answer: Private owners seek profit, so they have an incentive to cut costs and innovate; shareholders monitor managers; access to private capital for investment; competition if the market is opened.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: profit motive; 1 mark: cost cutting/investment [2]

items.stem: Explain two possible disadvantages of market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: Tax cuts may increase inequality and reduce revenue; deregulation may harm consumers or the environment; privatisation may create private monopolies; labour reforms may lower job security and wages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: The government of Loristan gives grants for research into green technology. What type of supply-side policy is this?
items.answer: Interventionist supply-side policy
items.markingKey: Interventionist supply-side policy: state support for research and development.

items.stem: The government of Jovania gives grants for research into green technology. What type of supply-side policy is this? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Interventionist supply-side policy: state support for research and development.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Interventionist supply-side policy; 1 mark: explanation – state support for research and development. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Productivity growth in Dravonia has been only 1.0% a year. The government plans to privatise the state railway, cut corporation tax, and raise spending on education to 4% of GDP. It hopes productivity growth will rise to 2.5%. Critics argue that privatisation will lead to higher fares and that tax cuts mainly benefit the rich. (a) Classify the three policies as market-based or interventionist. (b) Calculate the difference in output per worker after 10 years at the two productivity growth rates (start = 100).
items.answer: (a) Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. (b) 110.5 vs 128

items.stem: Which is a market-based supply-side policy?

items.answer: Higher post-tax profits increase funds and incentives for investment and attract FDI, raising the capital stock and LRAS.

options: Government spending on education and training
items.answer: Government spending on education and training

items.stem: Explain how government spending on education can increase long-run aggregate supply.
items.answer: It raises the skills and productivity of the labour force (human capital), increasing potential output and shifting LRAS to the right.

items.stem: Explain why interventionist supply-side policies may also increase aggregate demand.
items.answer: They involve government spending (G), which adds to AD in the short run before capacity effects appear.

items.answer: (a) $510bn; price level 108.35. (b) LRAS shifts right; with AD unchanged, equilibrium real output rises and the price level falls. (c) If AD rises faster than LRAS, the price level would still rise (inflation), though by less than without the reforms.

items.stem: Priya makes the following statement: ‘Supply-side policies quickly reduce cyclical unemployment.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Supply-side policies work slowly and raise capacity; cyclical unemployment is caused by low AD and needs demand-side measures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Supply-side policies work slowly and raise capacity; cyclical unemployment is caused by low AD and needs demand-side measures. [2]

items.stem: Supply-side reforms in Loristan raise full-employment output by 4% from $800bn. Aggregate demand is unchanged, and the price level falls by 1.5% from 110. Calculate the new full-employment output.

Supply-side reforms in Istrana raise full-employment output by 3% from $500bn. Aggregate demand is unchanged, and the price level falls by 1% from 100. (a) Calculate the new full-employment output and the new price level. (b) Using an AD/AS diagram, explain these changes. (c) Explain why the outcome might differ if AD were also rising quickly.
items.answer: (a) $515bn; price level 99. (b) LRAS shifts right; with AD unchanged, equilibrium real output rises and the price level falls. (c) If AD rises faster than LRAS, the price level would still rise (inflation), though by less than without the reforms.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) diagram explanation [1] (c) AD vs LRAS comparison [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Productivity growth in Calvania has been only 0.5% a year. The government plans to privatise the state railway, cut corporation tax, and raise spending on education to 5% of GDP. It hopes productivity growth will rise to 2.0%. Critics argue that privatisation will lead to higher fares and that tax cuts mainly benefit the rich. (a) Classify the three policies as market-based or interventionist. (b) Calculate the difference in output per worker after 10 years at the two productivity growth rates (start = 100). (c) Explain how higher education spending could increase LRAS. (d) Explain why privatisation might raise fares.
items.answer: (a) Privatisation and tax cut: market-based; education spending: interventionist. (b) 105.1 vs 121.9 (c) Human capital raises productivity and potential output. (d) A private monopoly seeks profit and may raise prices or cut services unless regulated.
